hints: Work on one side of the identity only, using double-angle formulae to express everything in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
Replace $\sin 2x$ by $2\sin x\cos x$ and $1-\cos 2x$ by an equivalent expression involving $\sin^2x$.
Factor the numerator and rewrite $\sin^2x$ as $(1-\cos x)(1+\cos x)$.
Cancel the common factor on the domain where the original expression is defined.
walkthrough:
Apply the double angle identities $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$ and $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$ to the left-hand side:
$$\text{Numerator: } 2\sin x - \sin 2x = 2\sin x - 2\sin x\cos x = 2\sin x(1 - \cos x)$$
$$\text{Denominator: } 1 - \cos 2x = 1 - (1 - 2\sin^2 x) = 2\sin^2 x$$

Form the fraction and simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by $2\sin x$:
$$\dfrac{2\sin x - \sin 2x}{1 - \cos 2x} = \dfrac{2\sin x(1 - \cos x)}{2\sin^2 x} = \dfrac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x}$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by $(1 + \cos x)$:
$$\dfrac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x} = \dfrac{(1 - \cos x)(1 + \cos x)}{\sin x(1 + \cos x)} = \dfrac{1 - \cos^2 x}{\sin x(1 + \cos x)}$$

Use the Pythagorean identity $1 - \cos^2 x = \sin^2 x$:
$$\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\sin x(1 + \cos x)} = \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$$

Conclude the required identity:
$$\dfrac{2\sin x - \sin 2x}{1 - \cos 2x} \equiv \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$$

ai_rubric.Trigonometric Identities: Double-angle identities rewrite the numerator and denominator in $\sin x$ and $\cos x$; cancellation of $1-\cos x$ gives $\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$.

hints: Use the identity from part (i) to simplify the integrand before integrating.
For $\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$, let $u=1+\cos x$ and account for the negative sign in $du$.
Evaluate the resulting logarithmic antiderivative at $\pi/2$ and $\pi/3$ in the correct order.
Use logarithm laws to combine the exact result into the form $\ln k$.
walkthrough:
Replace the integrand with the simplified form from part (i):
$$\int_{\frac{1}{3}\pi}^{\frac{1}{2}\pi} \dfrac{2\sin x - \sin 2x}{1 - \cos 2x}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_{\frac{1}{3}\pi}^{\frac{1}{2}\pi} \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Integrate using the substitution $u = 1 + \cos x$ where $\mathrm{d}u = -\sin x\,\mathrm{d}x$:
$$\int \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int \dfrac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u = -\ln|u| = -\ln(1 + \cos x)$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0$$
$$\text{Upper value} = -\ln(1 + 0) = -\ln 1 = 0$$

Evaluate the antiderivative at the lower limit $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\text{Lower value} = -\ln\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\int_{\frac{1}{3}\pi}^{\frac{1}{2}\pi} \dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 - \left(-\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$

State the answer in the form $\ln k$:
$$\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$

ai_rubric.Trigonometric Integration: Identifies an integral of the form $a\ln(1+\cos x)$; Derives $-\ln(1+\cos x)$; Concludes with $\ln\frac32$.
